subject: astronomy
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Stars near the celestial pole that never set below the horizon for a given observer are described as:
questions.explain: Circumpolar stars stay above the horizon all night as they appear to circle the celestial pole.

questions.q: Which group of stars are used by Northern Hemisphere observers to locate Polaris, the Pole Star?
options: The pointer stars of the Plough (Ursa Major)
questions.explain: The two 'pointer' stars at the end of the Plough (part of Ursa Major) line up with Polaris.

questions.q: A rock from space that survives its passage through the atmosphere and lands on the ground is called a:
questions.explain: A meteorite is the solid remnant that reaches the ground, whereas the streak of light in the sky is a meteor.

questions.q: On the celestial sphere, declination is the equivalent of which Earth coordinate?
questions.explain: Declination measures angular distance north or south of the celestial equator, like latitude on Earth.

questions.q: According to Newton, the gravitational force between two masses depends on distance how?
options: It increases with the square of the distance
It decreases with the square of the distance
questions.explain: Newton's law of gravitation is an inverse-square law: force falls off with the square of the distance.

questions.q: The bright, glowing head of gas and dust surrounding the nucleus of a comet is called the:
questions.explain: As a comet nears the Sun its ices vaporise, forming a glowing coma around the solid nucleus.

questions.q: How many planets are there in our solar system?
questions.explain: There are eight planets; Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.

questions.q: Which type of telescope is usually placed in space to observe radiation that is absorbed by the Earth's atmosphere, such as X-rays?
options: An X-ray telescope on a satellite
questions.explain: X-rays are blocked by the atmosphere, so X-ray telescopes must be flown above it on satellites in space.

questions.q: Which planet has the most prominent and visible ring system?
questions.explain: Saturn is famous for its bright, broad ring system made largely of ice particles.

questions.q: Increasing the aperture (diameter) of a telescope's objective mainly improves its ability to:
options: Collect more light and resolve finer detail
Increase the field of view only
questions.explain: A larger aperture gathers more light and improves resolving power, showing fainter, sharper detail.

questions.q: According to Kepler's third law, the square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the:
options: Cube of its average distance from the Sun
Square of its distance from the Sun
questions.explain: Kepler's third law states the period squared is proportional to the semi-major axis cubed, so distant planets take much longer to orbit.

questions.q: Most asteroids in the solar system are found in a belt located between:
questions.explain: The main asteroid belt lies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.

questions.q: One astronomical unit (AU) is defined as approximately the:
options: Distance light travels in one year
Average distance from the Earth to the Sun
Distance from the Earth to the Moon
questions.explain: An AU is the mean Earth-Sun distance, about 150 million kilometres.

questions.q: Stars appear to move across the night sky from east to west mainly because:
options: The Earth rotates on its axis from west to east
questions.explain: The apparent nightly motion of the stars is caused by the Earth's west-to-east rotation.

questions.q: A leap year, with 366 days, is added because:
options: The year is about 365.25 days, so an extra day keeps the calendar aligned
The Earth's orbit is slowing down
Of changes in the Earth's tilt
The Moon adds an extra day
questions.explain: Earth orbits the Sun in roughly 365.25 days, so an extra day every four years keeps the calendar in step.

questions.q: A planet moves fastest in its orbit when it is:
options: At a constant point regardless of distance
questions.explain: By Kepler's second law a planet moves fastest at perihelion, its closest approach to the Sun.

questions.q: A telescope has an objective of focal length 1000 mm and an eyepiece of focal length 20 mm. Its magnification is:
questions.explain: Magnification = focal length of objective / focal length of eyepiece = 1000 / 20 = 50.

questions.q: According to Kepler's first law, the orbit of a planet around the Sun is:
options: An ellipse with the Sun at the centre
An ellipse with the Sun at one focus
questions.explain: Kepler's first law states orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus, not the centre.

questions.q: Reflecting telescopes are generally preferred over refracting telescopes for very large instruments because mirrors:
options: Can be supported from behind and do not suffer chromatic aberration
questions.explain: Large mirrors can be supported across their backs and, unlike lenses, do not split colours (chromatic aberration), so reflectors scale to huge sizes.

questions.q: A reflecting telescope gathers light using a:
questions.explain: A reflector uses a concave primary mirror, avoiding the lens problems of large refractors.

questions.q: A refracting telescope forms its image using a:
questions.explain: A refractor uses a convex objective lens to gather and focus light; a reflector uses a mirror.

questions.q: Which group of planets are the gas giants?
questions.explain: The four outer planets Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are the gas (and ice) giants.
